answer.text: The claim is refuted. Reviews and observational research report that habitual knuckle cracking, including long-term and cumulative exposure, is not associated with clinical or radiographic osteoarthritis and does not appear to be a risk factor for hand osteoarthritis. [1][2] A review describes the belief that knuckle cracking causes arthritis as a myth, and another source states that there is no scientific evidence that it leads to osteoarthritis. [4][5] One study also found no immediate adverse findings after knuckle cracking. [3]
answer.short: Habitual knuckle cracking has not been shown to cause hand osteoarthritis or arthritis; available reviews and studies refute the claim. [1][2][4][5]

styled_answer.text: Refuted. The knuckle-cracking-causes-arthritis tale is more myth than medical menace: reviews and observational research find that habitual cracking, even long-term and cumulative, is not linked to clinical or radiographic osteoarthritis or hand osteoarthritis risk. [1][2] Reviews say there is no scientific evidence for the claim, and one study found no immediate adverse effects. [3][4][5]
styled_answer.short: Refuted: habitual knuckle cracking has not been shown to cause hand osteoarthritis or arthritis—the old warning is a myth, not evidence. [1][2][4][5]
